scenarios.title: Heavy Class Load
scenarios.text: Midterms in three classes the same week, and your position coach wants extra film sessions.

choices.label: Prioritize classes
choices.result: Straight A's on midterms.

choices.label: Prioritize football
choices.result: Your grades slip a little. Your kicking doesn't.

choices.label: Get a tutor and balance it
choices.result: Organized and on top of it.

scenarios.title: Roommate Trouble
scenarios.text: Your roommate games with friends until 3 a.m. every night.

choices.label: Set some ground rules
choices.result: Awkward talk, better sleep.

choices.label: Earplugs and ignore it
choices.result: You sleep. Sort of.

choices.label: Crash on a teammate's couch
choices.result: Fun, but your back hates you.

scenarios.title: Endorsement Offer
scenarios.text: Gridiron Grub, a local burger spot, wants you in a TV spot for a few hundred dollars.

choices.label: Sign and film it
choices.result: You're on TV. Your teammates won't let it go.

choices.label: Negotiate with the athletic department's help
choices.result: Better terms, less hassle.

choices.label: Pass and focus on the season
choices.result: Coach appreciates it.

scenarios.title: The Ad Drops
scenarios.text: Your Gridiron Grub commercial is running during every local broadcast.

choices.label: Lean into it
choices.result: Fans start chanting your catchphrase.

choices.label: Laugh it off and stay humble
choices.result: Teammates respect that.

scenarios.title: Team Tradition
scenarios.text: Upperclassmen tell the rookies to skip study hall and do a midnight 'team tradition' run around campus.

choices.label: Go along with it
choices.result: It's harmless, but you're exhausted and behind on school.

choices.label: Politely decline
choices.result: A few guys call you soft. Your grades thank you.

choices.label: Talk to the captain about it
choices.result: He makes it optional. Some rookies are grateful.

scenarios.title: Homesick
scenarios.text: First time this far from home. The dorm feels very quiet.

choices.label: Call home every night
choices.result: It helps. A lot.

choices.label: Join a study group
choices.result: New friends, better notes.

choices.label: Keep it to yourself
choices.result: It sits with you all week.

scenarios.title: Finals Crunch
scenarios.text: Two finals and a paper due the week of a big conference game.

choices.label: Pull an all-nighter
choices.result: Paper done. You are not.

choices.label: Study group every night
choices.result: Shared notes, shared stress.

choices.label: Ask for an extension
choices.result: Granted. A weight comes off.

scenarios.title: Media Day
scenarios.text: Cameras everywhere. Reporters want five minutes with the kicker.

choices.label: Prepared, polished answers
choices.result: Quotable and professional.

choices.label: Crack jokes the whole time
choices.result: The clip goes around campus.

choices.label: Keep it short
choices.result: You're back on the practice field in no time.

choices.label: Own the room
choices.result: The cameras love you. You walk out buzzing.

scenarios.title: New Coordinator, New Technique
scenarios.text: The new special teams coordinator wants to rebuild your approach angle.

choices.label: Rebuild it from scratch
choices.result: Awkward now. Better later.

choices.label: Keep your own style
choices.result: He's not thrilled, but your kicks are good.

choices.label: Meet him halfway
choices.result: Small tweaks that make sense.

scenarios.title: Internship or Training?
scenarios.text: A summer internship at a sports analytics firm, or a summer of full-time training?

choices.label: Take the internship
choices.result: You learn a ton. Your leg gets a little rusty.

choices.label: Train full-time
choices.result: Strongest you've ever been.

choices.label: Split the summer
choices.result: A bit of both.

scenarios.title: Scouts at Practice
scenarios.text: Pro scouts are timing your hang time at practice this week.

choices.label: Boom every kickoff
choices.result: Hang times the scouts can't ignore.

choices.label: Show your consistency
choices.result: Twenty straight through the middle.

choices.label: Talk shop with the scouts after
choices.result: They like how you think.

scenarios.title: Earn Your Spot
scenarios.text: As a walk-on, you're third on the depth chart. Coach says the job goes to whoever earns it in camp.

choices.label: Outkick the scholarship guy
choices.result: You win the job on the last day of camp.

choices.label: Learn everything from the starter
choices.result: He's impressed by how fast you learn.

choices.label: Ask coach exactly what he needs
choices.result: Clear goals, clear path.

scenarios.title: Combine Invite
scenarios.text: You've been invited to the pro scouting combine after the season.

choices.label: Train for the testing
choices.result: Your leg has never been stronger.

choices.label: Prepare for team interviews
choices.result: You'll walk in ready for every question.

choices.label: Stay focused on this season
choices.result: First things first.

scenarios.title: Academic Probation Warning
scenarios.text: The academic office warns you: below a 2.0 GPA you can't play.

choices.label: Daily tutoring
choices.result: Exhausting, but your grades climb.

choices.label: Drop your hardest class
choices.result: Breathing room.

choices.label: Hope for the best
choices.result: Hope is not a study plan.

scenarios.title: Move-In Day
scenarios.text: {parent} helps you haul boxes up three flights of stairs into a cinderblock dorm room. When everything's inside, he lingers by the door, jingling his keys, not quite ready to leave.

authoring.premise: {parent} helps you carry boxes into a cinderblock dorm room and lingers at the door longer than either of you expected.

choices.label: Promise to call every Sunday
choices.result: You hug him in the hallway and promise a call every Sunday night. He nods like it's a signed contract, and walking back to your room, you realize you meant it.

choices.label: Walk him to the car, quick
choices.result: You thank him, walk him to the car and wave before it's out of the lot. It's easier that way, though the room feels very quiet once you're back.

choices.label: Go over the plan one more time
choices.result: You sit on the bare mattress and walk through the plan you made together: the classes, the budget, the drive home at Thanksgiving. He leaves smiling, and so do you.
choices.lock_text: the college plan you made with your family

scenarios.title: The First Team Meeting
scenarios.text: {coach} runs the first special teams meeting like a courtroom: curfew at eleven, study hall signed in and out, phones in a bin by the door, and one strike before the coach calls home.

authoring.premise: {coach} lays out the rules on day one: curfew, study hall, phones in the bin at meetings, and one strike before the coach calls home.

choices.label: Write down every rule
choices.result: You write down every rule, including the ones nobody else bothers with. {coach} notices the notebook and nods once.

choices.label: Ask about the kickers' schedule
choices.result: You ask what the specialists' days look like. The answer runs long and a senior groans, but now you know exactly when you can kick on your own.

choices.label: Keep your phone in your pocket
choices.result: You keep it on silent in your pocket. It buzzes once during film, every head in the room turns, and the guys can't stop laughing. {coach} doesn't say a word, which is worse.

choices.label: Say you came ready to compete
choices.result: You tell {coach} you came in ready to compete now, not to wait your turn. The coach almost smiles and says the field will decide that.
choices.lock_text: being ready for college football

scenarios.title: Far From Home
scenarios.text: Three weeks in, the dining hall, the dorm and the practice field all feel like somebody else's life. Nobody here knew you before, and tonight that feels heavy.

authoring.premise: Three weeks in, the dining hall, the dorm and the practice field all feel like someone else's life, and nobody here knew you before.

choices.label: Build one routine that's yours
choices.result: You claim a corner table in the library and a bench by the practice field and go to both every day. It's small, but the campus starts to feel like it has a place for you.

choices.label: Call home and say it out loud
choices.result: You call {parent} and admit it's harder than you thought. He doesn't try to fix it; he just stays on the phone for an hour.

choices.label: Keep it to yourself
choices.result: You tell everyone you're fine and bury the feeling in extra kicking. The work piles up; the feeling doesn't go anywhere, it just gets quieter.

choices.label: Remember why you chose this place
choices.result: You pull up the list you made when you picked this school, far from home on purpose. Every reason is still true. You go to bed tired, but not lost.
choices.lock_text: having picked this school for your own reasons

scenarios.title: The Empty Group Chat
scenarios.text: Your high school group chat has gone quiet. {best_friend} keeps posting photos from a new school with new friends, and you realize you haven't texted anyone back home in a week.

authoring.premise: Your high school group chat goes quiet. {best_friend} posts photos from a new school with new friends, and you realize you haven't texted anyone in a week.

choices.label: Start a Sunday call
choices.result: You set up a Sunday video call for the old crew. Half of them show up the first week, and you laugh for an hour. It's a small thread back to home.

choices.label: Text {best_friend} directly
choices.result: You send {best_friend} a long message about how strange everything feels. The reply comes within a minute: same here.

choices.label: Lean into new friends
choices.result: You let the old chat sit and say yes to every invite on campus. Your new circle grows fast, though a few old friends stop checking in.

choices.label: Plan a visit like the old road trip
choices.result: You remember the campus trip you two took senior year and book a weekend to visit {best_friend}. The reply is three exclamation points.
choices.lock_text: a campus road trip with your best friend

scenarios.title: The Roommate Draw
scenarios.text: Your assigned roommate games with his headset on until four in the morning, laughing at things you can't see. Your first lift is at six.

authoring.premise: Your assigned roommate games until four in the morning, and your first lift is at six.

choices.label: Work out a deal
choices.result: You catch him at lunch and offer a trade: headphones and lights out by midnight on weeknights, and the room is his on weekends. He shrugs, then shakes on it.

choices.label: Freeze him out
choices.result: You stop talking to him and start letting the door slam at 5:30 every morning. It's a little satisfying, and by the second week the room feels like a hallway nobody wants to stand in.

choices.label: Sleep at the facility
choices.result: On lift nights you take a pillow to the athletes' lounge and get extra film in before bed. It works, mostly, though you never feel like you live anywhere.

scenarios.title: Mandatory Study Hall
scenarios.text: {teacher}, your academic advisor, hands you the schedule: six hours of study hall a week, signed in and out at the front desk. Miss them and your eligibility is the next conversation.

authoring.premise: Your academic advisor, {teacher}, sets your schedule: six hours of study hall a week, signed in and out, or you lose eligibility.

choices.label: Make them your best hours
choices.result: You treat study hall like practice: same seat, same time, phone in your bag. By midterms you're ahead in two classes.

choices.label: Sign in and do the minimum
choices.result: You sign in, put your head down and count the minutes. You get the hours and a few good naps, and not much else.

choices.label: Sign in and slip out
choices.result: A teammate shows you how to sign in and leave. It works for three weeks, until {teacher} notices the same handwriting on six lines of the sheet.

choices.label: Use what worked in high school
choices.result: You set up the same study blocks that saved your grades in high school. {teacher} looks at your plan and says you've clearly done this before. You have.
choices.lock_text: having pulled your grades back up before

scenarios.title: The Veteran Kicker
scenarios.text: The senior kicker you're replacing next year can make your first season easy or miserable, and he hasn't decided which. He kicks first, kicks last and doesn't say much.

authoring.premise: The senior kicker you're replacing next year can make your life easy or miserable, and he hasn't decided which.

choices.label: Ask him to teach you
choices.result: You ask if you can shadow his routine. He looks at you for a long second, then hands you his chart. By October you're warming up next to him every day.

choices.label: Outwork him quietly
choices.result: You show up before him and leave after him, every day. He notices. The coaches notice. Nobody says a word, and the air at the kicking net is thick.

choices.label: Keep your distance
choices.result: You stay polite and out of his way. It's peaceful, and you learn nothing from him at all.

scenarios.title: Walk-On Reality
scenarios.text: Scholarship players get meal cards, new cleats and a laptop. You get a locker and a parking ticket. In the weight room, a teammate jokes that walk-ons are practice dummies, and a few guys laugh.

authoring.premise: You're paying your own way while scholarship players get meal cards and gear you don't. A teammate jokes that walk-ons are practice dummies.

choices.label: Laugh it off and outwork them
choices.result: You laugh with them, then stay forty minutes after every lift for the rest of the week. Nobody says it again, mostly because they're tired of watching you.

choices.label: Say it back, calmly
choices.result: You tell him you're paying to be here, so you're probably the one who wants it most. The room goes quiet, then someone says, 'Fair.'

choices.label: Ask {coach} about a scholarship path
choices.result: After the lift you ask {coach}, plainly, what a walk-on has to do to earn a scholarship. The answer is long and honest, and you write it down.

scenarios.title: The Redshirt Teammate
scenarios.text: A freshman kicker who's redshirting this year sits out every game and watches you kick from the sideline in a sweatsuit. He's lonely, a little bitter, and very good.

authoring.premise: A freshman kicker who's redshirting this year sits out every game and watches you kick. He's lonely, bitter, and good.

choices.label: Make him your practice partner
choices.result: You ask him to chart your kicks while you chart his. By midseason you have the best practice partner on the roster, and he has a reason to show up.

choices.label: Compete with him every rep
choices.result: You turn every practice into a contest. It sharpens you both, and it makes the kicking net the tensest spot on the field.

choices.label: Leave him alone
choices.result: You figure he wants space and give it to him. He sits alone at team dinners for the rest of the season.

scenarios.title: The First Big Party
scenarios.text: Upperclassmen throw the first big party of the year on a Thursday night: loud music, a packed kitchen, plenty of drinking. The 6 a.m. lift is seven hours away, and everyone is watching what the freshmen do.

authoring.premise: Upperclassmen throw the first big party of the year on a Thursday. The 6 a.m. lift is in seven hours, and everyone is watching what the freshmen do.

choices.label: Stay an hour, then head out
choices.result: You meet half the team, laugh at the stories and slip out before midnight with a bottle of water. At six the next morning you're the only freshman who doesn't look gray.

choices.label: Skip it and sleep
choices.result: You tell the upperclassmen you've got the lift and go to bed. A couple of them call you soft, but you feel strong under the weights in the morning.

choices.label: Stay until it ends
choices.result: You're one of the last ones out at three. You make the lift, barely, and the strength coach writes your name on the whiteboard under LATE. The upperclassmen love you; the staff now knows your name for the wrong reason.

scenarios.title: Freshman Traditions
scenarios.text: After the first practice the seniors gather the freshmen and read out 'freshman duties': carry their bags on road trips, sing the fight song at team dinner, and fetch whatever they ask for, whenever they ask.

authoring.premise: The seniors announce freshman duties: carry their bags, sing the fight song at dinner, fetch whatever they ask for.

choices.label: Play along
choices.result: You carry the bags and sing badly at dinner. The seniors laugh, slap your back and learn your name a lot faster than anyone else's.

choices.label: Ask where the line is
choices.result: You ask a senior, politely, what happens if a freshman says no. The table goes quiet. He says nothing happens, but he says it like he's making a note.

scenarios.title: The Hazing Night
scenarios.text: Initiation night. The seniors line the freshmen up in the dark locker room, and it isn't singing anymore: there's a list of 'tests,' and one of them could get somebody hurt. The freshman next to you is shaking.

authoring.premise: The freshman 'initiation' night arrives, and it's not singing anymore. Some of what the seniors have planned is humiliating, and some of it could hurt someone.

choices.label: Call the hotline
choices.result: You step into the hallway and call the compliance number taped inside every locker. Twenty minutes later the lights come on and an assistant coach is standing in the doorway. Some of the seniors won't look at you for months.

choices.label: Walk out and take him with you
choices.result: You put a hand on the freshman's shoulder and walk him out. Nobody stops you, nobody follows, and the seniors make sure you hear about it all week.

choices.label: Go along with it
choices.result: You keep your head down and do what you're told. Nobody gets badly hurt, this time, but the next day the freshman won't sit anywhere near you in the dining hall.

scenarios.title: Long Distance
scenarios.text: {love_interest} is back home, and the calls keep getting shorter. Between practice, class and film, you've missed each other three nights in a row.

authoring.premise: {love_interest} is back home, the calls are getting shorter, and you keep missing each other between practice and class.

choices.label: Make a real schedule
choices.result: You set a call every Tuesday and Friday and guard them like practice. It isn't the same as being there, but it's something real to look forward to.

choices.label: Have the honest talk
choices.result: You call and say what you've both been avoiding: this isn't working from here. It's a hard, kind conversation, and it ends with both of you a little teary.

choices.label: Let it drift
choices.result: You keep meaning to call and keep not calling. Nothing ends, exactly. It just fades, and you spend the extra hours at the field.

scenarios.title: The Holiday You Miss
scenarios.text: The team practices straight through the holiday. {sibling} calls to ask why you're not coming home this year, and you can hear the whole family in the background.

authoring.premise: The team practices straight through the holiday. {sibling} calls to ask why you're not coming home this year.

choices.label: Join dinner by video
choices.result: You prop your phone against a water bottle and eat dining hall turkey while your family passes you around the table. {sibling} gives you a tour of the dessert you're missing.

choices.label: Promise {sibling} a real visit
choices.result: You promise {sibling} a weekend on campus in the spring, just the two of you. He holds you to it on the spot.

choices.label: Keep the call short
choices.result: You say hi to everyone, then say you've got film to watch. You do watch it, and you spend the rest of the night wishing you'd stayed on longer.

choices.label: Tell {parent} it's harder than you expected
choices.result: You step into the hallway and tell {parent} the truth: this one's hard. He tells you about his first holiday away from home, and it helps more than turkey would have.
choices.lock_text: having had the real talk with {parent}

scenarios.title: First Road Trip
scenarios.text: Your first road game: a hotel two states away, a bed check at eleven, and two upperclassmen in the next room planning to sneak out to a party across town. They want a freshman to come along.

authoring.premise: Your first road game: a hotel, a curfew check at eleven, and two upperclassmen planning to sneak out to a party across town.

choices.label: Stay in and lock in
choices.result: You stay in, watch film of tomorrow's stadium and are asleep by 11:15. The guys call you a rookie on the bus. You don't mind.

choices.label: Talk them out of it
choices.result: You tell them it isn't worth getting caught on the first trip. One of them listens; the other goes anyway and gets caught at the second bed check.

choices.label: Go with them
choices.result: You slip out the side door at midnight and get back at three, just ahead of the second bed check. The upperclassmen think you're fearless. In the morning, an assistant coach is reading the side door's alarm log.

scenarios.title: The Scholarship Fine Print
scenarios.text: Your aid paperwork has a line you skipped in August: keep a minimum GPA or lose part of it. Midterms are in three weeks, and you haven't opened two of your textbooks.

authoring.premise: Your aid paperwork comes with a line you skipped: a minimum GPA to keep it. Midterms are in three weeks.

choices.label: Build a grade plan now
choices.result: You map out every assignment between now and finals and book two tutoring sessions. It eats your free evenings, but by midterms you're on solid ground.

choices.label: Ask the aid office to explain it
choices.result: You walk to the financial aid office and ask them to explain the number in plain English. It's less scary than you thought, and now you know exactly where the line is.

choices.label: Figure it out later
choices.result: You tell yourself you'll catch up after the next road trip. The road trip comes and goes, and so does the catching up.

choices.label: Line it up with your academic scholarship
choices.result: You pull out the terms of the academic scholarship you earned in high school and line them up with your athletic aid. Both ask for the same thing: grades you already know how to keep.
choices.lock_text: a secured academic scholarship

scenarios.title: The Pattern
scenarios.text: You owned your first mistake, and the staff believed you. Now there's another one, and {coach} wants to know whether that first apology meant anything.

authoring.premise: You owned your first mistake, and the staff believed you. Now there's another one, and {coach} wants to know whether the first apology meant anything.
authoring.note: Opens only on a strike after owning the first one (The Coach's Office clears strikes). The good choice sets owned_it_again and second_chance_used; the bad one sets character_concerns. Story event (x4 weight while open; forced in the last week of its window if the player qualifies): forced in year 4 week 6.

choices.label: Own it again, and change something
choices.result: You don't explain it away. You tell {coach} what happened, what you'll change and who can hold you to it. The coach is quiet for a long time, then says this is the last time this conversation is a conversation.

choices.label: Say it was different this time
choices.result: You explain why this one isn't like the first one. {coach} listens to all of it and doesn't believe any of it, and you can see the moment the coach stops trusting what you say.

scenarios.title: The Sports Psychologist
scenarios.text: The athletic department offers every player free sessions with the team's sports psychologist. Most of the locker room jokes about it, and you've been lying awake replaying kicks you haven't even attempted yet.

authoring.premise: The athletic department offers every player sessions with a sports psychologist. Most of the team jokes about it.

choices.label: Book a session
choices.result: You sign up for a Tuesday slot and nearly cancel twice. It's just talking: about sleep, about pressure, about home. You leave with a breathing routine and a second appointment.

choices.label: Ask a senior who goes
choices.result: You quietly ask a senior you've heard goes every week. He says it changed how he handles game days and offers to walk over with you next time.

choices.label: Laugh it off with the guys
choices.result: You join the jokes in the locker room and don't sign up. It's easier for now, though the sleepless nights keep coming.

scenarios.title: Homecoming Weekend
scenarios.text: Homecoming weekend. Alumni pack the campus, boosters want photos, the band wants the specialists for a halftime skit at Friday's pep rally, and the team wants you in bed by ten.

authoring.premise: Alumni pack the campus for homecoming. Boosters want photos, the band wants the specialists for a skit, and the team wants you rested.

choices.label: Do the skit
choices.result: You learn the dance in an hour and do it in front of five thousand people. It's ridiculous, the clip goes around campus, and the band adopts you.

choices.label: Do the booster photos
choices.result: You spend an hour smiling for alumni photos. One of them owns the business you've wanted to intern at, and he gives you his card.

choices.label: Skip it all and rest
choices.result: You eat, stretch and are asleep by nine while the campus loses its mind outside your window.

scenarios.title: The Booster's Handshake
scenarios.text: A friendly booster shakes your hand after practice and leaves something in it: a prepaid card 'for a nice dinner, on me.' You know the compliance rules, and so does he.

authoring.premise: A friendly booster shakes your hand after practice and leaves something in it: a prepaid card 'for a nice dinner.'

choices.label: Hand it back
choices.result: You hand the card back with a smile and say compliance would have your head. He laughs, a little embarrassed, and doesn't try again.

choices.label: Turn it in to compliance
choices.result: You walk the card to the compliance office the same afternoon. They thank you, and the booster stops showing up at practice.

choices.label: Keep it
choices.result: You pocket it and take three teammates to the best steakhouse in town. Two weeks later compliance asks every freshman about gifts, and the booster's name comes up.

scenarios.title: The First NIL Pitch
scenarios.text: A local sandwich shop offers you your first NIL deal: free lunch all season and a post a week. It's legal and approved, but it's your face in their window.

authoring.premise: A local sandwich shop offers a small deal: free food all season and a few posts. It's legal, but it's your name on it.

choices.label: Sign it
choices.result: You sign, take a photo by the counter and eat better than anyone on the team. A few teammates tease you about the poster in the window.

choices.label: Run it by compliance first
choices.result: You bring it to {coach} and the compliance office before you sign. It takes a week and the deal is approved anyway, but now everyone knows you do things right.

choices.label: Pass for now
choices.result: You thank the owner and say you want to focus on your first season. He says the offer stands whenever you're ready.

choices.label: Mention your hometown work
choices.result: You mention the volunteer work back home that earned you a reference letter, and the owner doubles the deal on the spot: he wants the kid who helps out.
choices.lock_text: a community reference from home

scenarios.title: Budget Week
scenarios.text: Midterms, and your account is nearly empty. Rent, books and the phone bill are all due the same week, and you've been eating cereal for dinner since Sunday.

authoring.premise: It's the middle of the semester and your account is nearly empty. Rent, books and a phone bill are due the same week.

choices.label: Call {parent}
choices.result: You call {parent} and ask for help. He doesn't hesitate, and you hear how tight things are at home in the way he says 'it's fine.'

choices.label: Pick up a weekend shift
choices.result: You find a Saturday-morning shift at the campus bookstore. It eats your one free morning, and it covers the phone bill.

choices.label: Make a real budget
choices.result: You sit down with the team's financial-literacy person and build a budget for the rest of the semester. It's not fun. It works.

choices.label: Use the savings
choices.result: You dip into the savings you started with your first paycheck in high school. It covers the week, and you start a new rule: never below a hundred dollars.
choices.lock_text: having saved your first paychecks

scenarios.title: The Kicker You Know
scenarios.text: {tyler} is a college kicker now too, and your names keep landing next to each other: the same freshman watch list, the same conference, the same comment threads arguing about who's better.

authoring.premise: {tyler} is a college kicker now too, and your names keep showing up next to each other on the same lists.

choices.label: Text him congratulations
choices.result: You text {tyler} about the watch list and tell him to leave some room at the top. He writes back that he'll see you there. It's good to know someone else gets it.

choices.label: Let the threads fire you up
choices.result: You read every thread and screenshot the worst ones about you. Practice gets an extra edge, and so do you.

choices.label: Ignore the noise
choices.result: You mute the threads and never mention his name. You sleep fine, and your kicking stays your own.

choices.label: Call him like old times
choices.result: You call {tyler} and talk for an hour about the old net sessions and your new coaches. You hang up feeling less alone in all of it.
choices.lock_text: having trained with {tyler} in high school

scenarios.title: The New Holder
scenarios.text: Your new holder, {holder}, spins the laces toward the goalposts a different way than you're used to. You've each done it your own way for years, and neither of you wants to be the one to change.

authoring.premise: Your new holder, {holder}, spins the laces a different way than you're used to, and neither of you wants to be the one to change.

choices.label: Change to {holder}'s way
choices.result: You adjust your approach to the new laces. The first week is ugly in practice, and by the second, you've stopped noticing.

choices.label: Ask {holder} to change
choices.result: You explain why the laces matter to your contact and ask {holder} to switch. It's done, a little stiffly.

choices.label: Chart both ways
choices.result: You suggest fifty reps each way, charted, and let the numbers decide. It costs a week of practice, and nobody has to win the argument.

choices.label: Tell {holder} what trust looks like
choices.result: You tell {holder} about the high school holder who never let you down and what that trust looked like. Then you ask what {holder} needs from you. You figure out the laces together by Friday.
choices.lock_text: having trusted a holder in a big moment before

scenarios.title: Sleepless Before Saturday
scenarios.text: You haven't slept more than four hours before a game all season. You lie awake at 2 a.m. replaying kicks you haven't even tried yet.

authoring.premise: You haven't slept more than four hours before a game all season. You lie awake replaying kicks you haven't attempted yet.

choices.label: Tell the team trainer
choices.result: You tell the trainer, who doesn't laugh. You leave with a sleep routine, a no-screens rule and the number for the team's sports psychologist.

choices.label: Watch film until you're tired
choices.result: You watch special teams film until your eyes close. You sleep a little more and dream about protection schemes.

choices.label: Just push through
choices.result: You decide it's part of the job and stop thinking about it. Some nights that works. Most nights it doesn't, so you fill them with extra film.

scenarios.title: The Class You're Failing
scenarios.text: A D on your chemistry midterm. {teacher} sees every athlete's grades on Friday, whether you mention it or not.

authoring.premise: A D on your chemistry midterm. Your advisor will see it Friday whether you tell them or not.

choices.label: Hope it gets lost
choices.result: You don't mention it and hope it slips through. It doesn't, and when {teacher} brings it up, it's the hiding that makes the conversation hard.

choices.label: Tell {teacher} first
choices.result: You walk into the office Thursday with the test in your hand. By the end of the meeting you have a tutor, a study table time and a plan.

choices.label: Fix it yourself
choices.result: You go to the professor's office hours twice a week and redo every problem you missed. You don't tell anyone, and the final goes better than anyone expected.

scenarios.title: Group Project Ghost
scenarios.text: A teammate in your class wants his name on your group project. He hasn't come to a single meeting, and the other two in your group are looking at you to decide.

authoring.premise: A teammate in your class wants his name on your group project. He hasn't come to a single meeting.

choices.label: Leave his name off
choices.result: You tell the group his name stays off unless he does a section. He's cold to you at practice for a week.

choices.label: Give him one real job
choices.result: You give him the slides and a deadline. He does them, badly, at 2 a.m., and he shows up to the next meeting.

choices.label: Put his name on it
choices.result: You add his name and do his part yourself. It's easier than the argument, the project gets an A, and the rest of your group notices.

choices.label: Remember how covering went last time
choices.result: You covered for a teammate once in high school and remember how that went. You tell him plainly: show up Thursday, or his name stays off. He shows up, and you spend Thursday night catching him up.
choices.lock_text: having covered for a teammate before

scenarios.title: The Captain's Talk
scenarios.text: The senior captain pulls you aside after practice: some of the guys think you act like you're too good for the team. Specialists eat together, stretch together and leave together.

authoring.premise: The senior captain pulls you aside: some of the guys think you act like you're too good for the team.

choices.label: Eat with the linemen
choices.result: For the next two weeks you sit at a different table every lunch. The linemen adopt you first; they say kickers are 'basically mascots,' affectionately.

choices.label: Ask what he means
choices.result: You ask the captain for specifics instead of guessing. It turns out to be one thing, leaving lifts early, and you fix it the next day.

choices.label: Keep your routine
choices.result: You say your routine is what makes you good and keep it. The captain shrugs, and the comments don't stop.

scenarios.title: The Highlight Clip
scenarios.text: A trick-shot clip of you from practice, the ball off the crossbar and into a trash can, goes around campus. Suddenly people you've never met want a picture.

authoring.premise: A trick-shot clip of you from practice goes around campus, and suddenly people you don't know want a picture.

choices.label: Make a few more
choices.result: You film a series of trick shots with the specialists on Sunday afternoons. The account grows, and so does the time it takes.

choices.label: Enjoy it and move on
choices.result: You take the pictures, thank people and don't film another one. It fades in a week, the way these things do.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what's okay to post
choices.result: You ask {coach} where the line is. The coach likes the question and sends you the team's social media guide.

scenarios.title: The Online Comment
scenarios.text: A fan account tears into you on Sunday: your form, your scholarship, your family. Your thumb is already on the reply button.

authoring.premise: A fan account tears into you after a loss. Your thumb is already on the reply button.

choices.label: Reply with exactly what you think
choices.result: You write it, send it and feel great for about ten minutes. By morning the screenshot is everywhere, and the athletic department's social media office wants a word.

choices.label: Put the phone down
choices.result: You put the phone in a drawer and go for a walk. It still stings the next day. It doesn't follow you anywhere.

choices.label: Mute the account and tell the staff
choices.result: You mute the account and send a screenshot to the team's media staff. They handle the part about your family; you never see it again.

choices.label: Do what worked before
choices.result: You dealt with something like this in high school, so you don't reply. You write the reply in your notes app, read it twice and delete it.
choices.lock_text: having handled an old post the right way before

scenarios.title: {parent}'s Phone Call
scenarios.text: {parent} sounds tired on the phone. His hours got cut at work, he says, but it's nothing for you to worry about.

authoring.premise: {parent} sounds tired on the phone. His hours got cut, he says, but it's nothing for you to worry about.

choices.label: Offer to help
choices.result: You say you could pick up a job, send money, anything. He says no, firmly. He also says it means a lot that you asked.

choices.label: Take him at his word
choices.result: You say okay and turn the conversation to your week. He sounds relieved to talk about something else, and you keep your mind on school and football.

choices.label: Ask the real numbers
choices.result: You've helped at home before, so you ask how short the month is. He tells you, finally. You send what you can and agree to talk every Sunday.
choices.lock_text: having helped your family with money before

scenarios.title: The Sibling Visit
scenarios.text: {sibling} comes to campus for a weekend and wants to see everything: the locker room, the dorm and the parties he's heard about from his friends.

authoring.premise: {sibling} comes to campus for a weekend and wants to see everything: the locker room, the dorm, the parties he's heard about.

choices.label: Give him the real tour
choices.result: You show him the locker room, the film room and the dining hall at midnight, then watch a movie in your dorm. He says it's the best weekend of his year.

choices.label: Take him to the team barbecue
choices.result: You bring him to the team's Saturday barbecue, where linemen teach him to throw a spiral. It's loud and safe, and he talks about it for months.

choices.label: Say no to the parties, and why
choices.result: You tell him there's no party tour and explain why, without a lecture. He sulks for an hour, then asks if you can play video games instead.

scenarios.title: The Upperclassman's Notes
scenarios.text: An upperclassman offers you a copy of this semester's chemistry midterm, the real one, before the professor gives it. 'Everybody uses them,' he says.

authoring.premise: An upperclassman offers you a folder of last year's exams for your hardest class. 'Everybody uses them,' he says.

choices.label: Take the folder
choices.result: You accept the folder. You score an A on the midterm, and a month later the professor changes the final, catches the pattern in the answers and reports half the class.

choices.label: Say no and study
choices.result: You say no thanks and spend Thursday night with the practice problems. You get a C-plus, and it's yours.

choices.label: Tell {teacher}
choices.result: You don't name him, but you tell {teacher} the midterm is out there. The professor writes a new exam, and nobody ever knows it was you.

scenarios.title: Winter Conditioning
scenarios.text: Winter conditioning starts at 5:30 a.m., in the dark, in the snow. Three teammates have already started skipping and signing each other in on the attendance sheet, and they've offered to sign you in too.

authoring.premise: Winter workouts start at 5:30 a.m. in the dark. Three teammates have already started skipping and signing each other in.

choices.label: Let them sign you in
choices.result: You sleep in twice. The third time, the strength coach checks the sheet against the door cameras, and every name on it gets a phone call home and a meeting with {coach}.

choices.label: Show up every morning
choices.result: You're there at 5:30 every day for six weeks. By February, you're the one the freshmen follow across the parking lot.

choices.label: Show up and bring them
choices.result: You start knocking on their doors at 5:10. Two of them start coming. The third stops answering the door.

choices.label: Add your own plan on top
choices.result: You show up every morning and add the plan you've kept since high school in the evenings. It's a lot, and by spring your leg feels like somebody else's.
choices.lock_text: having built your own training plan before

scenarios.title: Spring Kicking Competition
scenarios.text: Spring practice opens with a kicking competition for next season. The veteran kicker is graduating, the job is open, and {coach} will chart every kick for three weeks.

authoring.premise: Spring practice opens with a kicking competition for next season. The veteran kicker is graduating, and the job is wide open.

choices.label: Treat it like a job interview
choices.result: You show up early, chart your own kicks next to {coach}'s chart and ask for feedback after every session. By the end, the coach is asking you what you see.

choices.label: Kick loose and have fun with it
choices.result: You treat it like a backyard contest and trash-talk the other kickers all spring. It keeps you relaxed, and it doesn't make {coach} smile.

choices.label: Help the other kickers too
choices.result: You share your warmup with the other kickers in the competition, even the one chasing your spot. The room gets better, and so do they.

scenarios.title: The Coach's Office
scenarios.text: {coach} closes the office door and slides a printed report across the desk. Word of what happened got back to the staff. 'I want to hear it from you,' the coach says, 'before I decide what happens next.'

authoring.premise: {coach} closes the door. Word of what you did got back to the staff, and the coach wants to hear it from you before deciding anything.
authoring.note: Story event (x4 weight while open; forced in the last week of its window if the player qualifies): forced in year 3 week 11.

choices.label: Tell the whole truth
choices.result: You don't trim anything. {coach} listens without interrupting, then hands you a list: three 6 a.m. workouts with the strength staff and a talk with the team. 'That's the end of it, if it stays the end of it.'

choices.label: Shrink your part in it
choices.result: You say you were barely involved and that other people pushed it. {coach} nods slowly and writes something down. You walk out without a punishment and with the feeling you just made things worse.

scenarios.title: The Tutor Who Offers More
scenarios.text: Your tutor glances at your history paper, sighs and offers to 'clean it up' before Friday. You both know that means writing it.

authoring.premise: Your tutor offers to 'clean up' your history paper. You both know that means writing it.

choices.label: Write it yourself
choices.result: You thank the tutor, ask for feedback instead and rewrite the paper over two late nights. It's a B-minus, and every word of it is yours.

choices.label: Ask for an extension
choices.result: You email your professor and ask for three more days because of travel. You get two, and the paper is better for them.

choices.label: Let the tutor 'clean it up'
choices.result: You hand it over. It comes back sharp, clever and nothing like the way you write. Your professor notices that too, and the grade comes back lower than the draft would have earned.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Prescription
scenarios.text: Your hip has ached for a week, and every kickoff makes it worse. In the locker room a teammate shakes a few tablets out of his prescription bottle and holds them out. 'Takes the edge off,' he says. 'Everybody does it.'

authoring.premise: Your hip is sore, and a teammate offers you some of his prescription. 'It's basically nothing,' he says.

choices.label: Tell the trainer about the hip
choices.result: You hand them back and walk to the training room. The trainer finds an inflamed hip flexor, cuts your kicking reps for a week and starts you on rehab. Your teammate rolls his eyes, but your hip feels better by Friday.

choices.label: Turn him down and ice it
choices.result: You say no thanks, ice the hip every night and keep it to yourself. It doesn't get worse, but it doesn't get better, and every kickoff stings.

choices.label: Say nothing and cover for him
choices.result: You don't take them, but when the trainer asks the team whether anyone has been sharing medication, you say you haven't seen a thing. Two weeks later a freshman ends up in the training room, and the staff learns who knew.

scenarios.title: The Big House Party
scenarios.text: An off-campus party gets out of hand fast: too many people, a broken window, and someone saying campus security is on the way. A teammate who's in bad shape can't find his ride.

authoring.premise: An off-campus party gets out of hand fast. Campus security is on the way, and a teammate who's in bad shape can't find his ride.

choices.label: Get him home
choices.result: You find his phone, call an older teammate with a car and get him home before security arrives. You spend the rest of the night making sure he's okay.

choices.label: Leave before it gets worse
choices.result: You grab your jacket and walk out the back before the lights come on. You're asleep by midnight, and the story on Monday doesn't have your name in it.

choices.label: Stay for the chaos
choices.result: You stay until security shows up and the names get written down, yours included. It's a legendary night for about a day, until the athletic department gets the list.

scenarios.title: Hazing Fallout
scenarios.text: The athletic department opens an investigation into last year's initiation night. Investigators want to talk to every sophomore, one at a time, and the seniors who ran it are watching who goes in.

authoring.premise: The athletic department opens an investigation into last year's initiation night, and investigators want to talk to every sophomore.

choices.label: Tell them everything
choices.result: You tell the investigators exactly what you saw, names included. The tradition is shut down by the end of the month. A few people in the locker room never forgive you, and a few quietly thank you.

choices.label: Answer only what they ask
choices.result: You answer every question honestly and volunteer nothing. It's true and it's safe, and you walk out not sure it was enough.

choices.label: Close ranks
choices.result: You tell them you don't remember much. The investigation stalls, the seniors nod at you in the hallway, and you know exactly what you did.

scenarios.title: Now You're the Upperclassman
scenarios.text: The new freshmen arrive, and the seniors look at your class. Freshman duties are yours to run this year, or yours to end.

authoring.premise: The new freshmen arrive, and the seniors look at your class. Freshman duties are yours to run now, or to end.

choices.label: End it
choices.result: You and two classmates tell the seniors your class won't run it. There's grumbling for a week, then something new: the freshmen get a real welcome dinner instead.

choices.label: Keep it, but lighter
choices.result: You keep the bag-carrying and the fight song and drop everything else. The freshmen laugh along, mostly. The seniors say your class went soft.

scenarios.title: The New Freshman Kicker
scenarios.text: {coach} signs a scholarship freshman kicker, {backup}, and assigns them to share your reps and your row in the locker room. {backup} is quiet, nervous, and has a much bigger leg than you expected.

authoring.premise: {coach} signs a scholarship freshman kicker, {backup}, and assigns them to share your reps and your locker row.

choices.label: Show {backup} the ropes
choices.result: You walk {backup} through the specialists' schedule, the film room and which upperclassmen to avoid. It costs you a few reps, and {backup} starts asking you questions instead of the coaches.

choices.label: Keep {backup} at arm's length
choices.result: You stay polite and give {backup} nothing extra. Your reps stay your reps, and the kicking net gets very quiet.

scenarios.title: The Position Battle
scenarios.text: Fall camp turns into a public competition with {backup}. Every kick is charted on a whiteboard by the locker room door, and the depth chart comes out Friday.

authoring.premise: Fall camp turns into a public competition with {backup}. Every kick is charted, and the depth chart comes out Friday.

choices.label: Compete clean
choices.result: You kick your best, congratulate {backup}'s good ones and let the chart speak. Friday, your name is still on top, and the room respects how it got there.

choices.label: Get in {backup}'s head
choices.result: You mention, casually, how the last backup cracked under the camp pressure. {backup} misses two in a row that afternoon. You keep the job; you lose some of the room.

scenarios.title: The High School Tape
scenarios.text: {coach} rewatches your old recruiting tape and stops on one clip: a long kick in perfect conditions with the distance marker cropped out. 'Tell me about this one,' the coach says.

authoring.premise: {coach} rewatches your old recruiting tape and stops on one clip. 'Tell me about this one,' the coach says.

choices.label: Tell the truth about the clip
choices.result: You say it was a practice kick, wind at your back, and the crop was your idea. {coach} nods slowly and says the honest answer is worth more than the clip.

choices.label: Shrug and change the subject
choices.result: You say it was a long time ago and ask about this week's practice plan. {coach} lets it go, and doesn't forget it.

choices.label: Stop defending it
choices.result: You defended that clip once to a high school coach. This time you don't. You tell {coach} the whole thing, including the defending.
choices.lock_text: having defended that clip in high school

choices.label: Say you fixed it years ago
choices.result: You tell {coach} you caught it in high school and sent the corrected version to every coach. The coach checks the files, finds it, and smiles.
choices.lock_text: having corrected that video in high school

scenarios.title: Did I Pick Right?
scenarios.text: Friends at other schools look happier in every post, and a teammate keeps talking about the transfer portal like it's an escape hatch. You find yourself scrolling other teams' rosters at night.

authoring.premise: Friends at other schools look happier, and a teammate keeps talking about the transfer portal like it's an escape hatch.

choices.label: Recommit out loud
choices.result: You tell {coach} you're all in here, and you mean it. Saying it makes the doubts quieter, and the coach remembers that you said it.

choices.label: Keep your options open
choices.result: You start reading about other programs and how the portal works. Nothing's decided, but your mind is half somewhere else.

choices.label: Talk it through with {parent}
choices.result: You call {parent} and say it plainly: you don't know if you picked right. He listens, then asks what would actually be different somewhere else. You don't have a good answer.

choices.label: Admit you never really decided
choices.result: You realize you came here without ever fully deciding, and that's the real problem. You sit down and decide now, on purpose. It feels like the first day all over again, in a good way.
choices.lock_text: never having fully decided where you belonged

scenarios.title: The Portal Call
scenarios.text: A coach from another school calls your phone directly, which isn't allowed. He says there's a spot for you if you ever 'get curious,' and he'd love to talk numbers.

authoring.premise: A coach from another school calls you directly, which isn't allowed. He says there's a spot for you if you ever 'get curious.'

choices.label: Report the call
choices.result: You tell {coach} and the compliance office about the call the same day. It's awkward, and it's the right thing; the other school gets a letter.

choices.label: Hang up and forget it
choices.result: You say you're not interested and hang up. You don't tell anyone, and you don't think about it again, mostly.

choices.label: Hear him out
choices.result: You listen to the pitch and agree to 'stay in touch.' A week later a compliance officer asks you why that coach's number is in your call log.

scenarios.title: The Sophomore Slump
scenarios.text: Your practice charts are the worst they've been since high school. You can't stop thinking about it: in class, at dinner, at two in the morning.

authoring.premise: Your practice charts are the worst they've been since high school, and you can't stop thinking about it, even in class.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what's changed
choices.result: You bring your chart to {coach} and ask straight out what's wrong. The answer is small and fixable: your plant foot has drifted. Knowing that helps more than any pep talk.

choices.label: Grind through it alone
choices.result: You don't tell anyone and add a hundred kicks a day. Your leg gets tired, your head gets louder, and the charts barely move.

choices.label: Take a weekend off
choices.result: You leave the bag at the facility for two days and do nothing football. You come back looser, and the first few kicks feel like yours again.

choices.label: Go back to the sports psychologist
choices.result: You book the Tuesday slot again and talk through the slump. You leave with a reset routine for bad days, and Thursday's charting looks like you.
choices.lock_text: having worked with the sports psychologist

scenarios.title: Panic in the Tunnel
scenarios.text: In the tunnel before warmups your chest goes tight, your hands won't stop shaking, and you can't get a full breath. The other specialists are already jogging onto the field.

authoring.premise: Before warmups your chest goes tight, your hands won't stop shaking and you can't get a full breath.

choices.label: Tell the trainer what's happening
choices.result: You grab the trainer's arm and say it out loud. She walks you through slow breathing behind the bench until it passes, and on Monday she sets you up with the team's counselor.

choices.label: Ask {holder} for a minute
choices.result: You tell {holder} you need a minute. {holder} stands with you, talking about nothing, until your breathing slows.

choices.label: Push it down and go
choices.result: You clench your fists, say nothing and jog out. You get through warmups on autopilot and spend the night wondering when it will happen again.

scenarios.title: The Injury You Can't Hide
scenarios.text: A groin strain flares on every kickoff. The trainer wants you out of kicking drills for a week; the season, and the backup kicker watching you warm up, say otherwise.

authoring.premise: A groin strain flares on every kickoff. The trainer wants you out a week; the season says otherwise.

choices.label: Follow the trainer's plan
choices.result: You sit out a week of drills and do every band exercise the trainer gives you. It's maddening, but you come back without the pull.

choices.label: Kick through it, carefully
choices.result: You keep kicking with a shorter run-up and ice twice a day. You get your reps, and the strain stays exactly as bad as it was.

choices.label: Hide it from the staff
choices.result: You tell the trainer it's fine and tape it yourself. It holds for a week, until a long kickoff in practice leaves you limping off the field in front of everyone.

choices.label: Do the rehab the right way
choices.result: You've done this before, so you build the rehab week yourself and show it to the trainer, who barely changes a thing. You're back to full speed in five days.
choices.lock_text: having done a full rehab before

scenarios.title: The Training Table
scenarios.text: A guy at the gym swears by a powder that 'adds five yards in a month.' It isn't on the team's approved list, and two teammates already keep a tub of it in their lockers.

authoring.premise: A guy at the gym swears by a powder that isn't on the team's approved list. Two teammates already use it.

choices.label: Ask the team dietitian
choices.result: You bring the label to the team dietitian, who reads it twice and tells you exactly why it's banned. She builds you a real plan instead, and it's slower and it works.

choices.label: Stick to the weight room
choices.result: You pass on the powder and add one more heavy lift day. No shortcuts, no surprises, just sore legs.

choices.label: Order it and say nothing
choices.result: It shows up in a plain bag. A week later the strength staff runs a locker check before a random test, finds it on your shelf, and you spend an hour in compliance explaining something you can't.

scenarios.title: The Visit Home
scenarios.text: You go home for the first time in months. Your old room is a storage closet now, {parent} has a new routine you don't know, and {best_friend} keeps talking about people you've never met.

authoring.premise: You go home for the first time in months. Your old room is a storage closet now, and everyone talks about people you don't know.

choices.label: Ask about the new stuff
choices.result: You ask {parent} about his new routine and {best_friend} about the new friends, and you mean it. By the end of the week, you're in some of the stories.

choices.label: Bring back the old routine
choices.result: You talk {best_friend} into the old diner, the old field and the old jokes. It's good, and it's a little like visiting a museum.

choices.label: Cut the trip short
choices.result: You go back to campus two days early and spend them in the weight room. It's easier than feeling like a guest at home.

scenarios.title: Someone New
scenarios.text: A classmate from your statistics class asks if you want to study together before the midterm, and it doesn't feel like it's only about studying.

authoring.premise: A classmate from your statistics class asks if you want to study together, and it doesn't feel like it's only about studying.

choices.label: Say yes
choices.result: You meet at the library and spend more time talking than studying. You both pass the midterm, and you have a standing Thursday night after that.

choices.label: Keep it to studying
choices.result: You say yes to the study session and keep it about statistics. It's friendly and useful, and you both ace the midterm.

choices.label: Say the season comes first
choices.result: You thank them and say your schedule is too full right now. It's true, and it still stings a little on the walk home.

scenarios.title: The Best Friend's Crisis
scenarios.text: {best_friend} calls at midnight, barely holding it together: they're failing out of school and haven't told their family. They don't know who else to call.

authoring.premise: {best_friend} calls at midnight: they're failing out of school and haven't told their family.

choices.label: Drive there this weekend
choices.result: You drive four hours on your only free Saturday and spend it at {best_friend}'s kitchen table, sorting out what can still be saved. You get back late Sunday, exhausted and glad you went.

choices.label: Stay on the phone and make a plan
choices.result: You stay on the phone until two, writing down every class, every deadline and every person who could help. By the end, {best_friend} has a list and sounds a little steadier.

choices.label: Point them to someone who can help
choices.result: You tell {best_friend} to call their academic advisor in the morning and promise to check in tomorrow. It's sensible advice, and it sounds smaller than you meant it to.

scenarios.title: {parent} Loses His Job
scenarios.text: {parent} finally tells you: the cut hours turned into a layoff. He says he'll figure it out. You have a little NIL money in the bank and a semester of books still to buy.

authoring.premise: {parent} finally tells you: the cut hours became a layoff. He says he'll figure it out.

choices.label: Send money home
choices.result: You send most of what you have and don't tell anyone on the team. {parent} calls to argue, then to say thank you.

choices.label: Keep it for school
choices.result: You talk it through with {parent}, and he insists: keep it for books and rent, so he doesn't have to worry about you too. You do, and you call every Sunday.

choices.label: Send half, keep half
choices.result: You split it down the middle. It doesn't solve either problem, and it helps both a little.

scenarios.title: The Collective
scenarios.text: The school's NIL collective offers a monthly deal: appearances at booster dinners, a few posts and a check. It's real money, and it's a lot of evenings in a nice shirt.

authoring.premise: The school's NIL collective offers a monthly deal for appearances at booster events. It's real money, and it's a lot of evenings.

choices.label: Sign with the collective
choices.result: You sign and spend two evenings a month shaking hands at booster dinners. The money helps, and a few of those boosters start showing up to practice to watch you.

choices.label: Ask to cap the appearances
choices.result: You ask for half the appearances at half the money. The collective agrees, a little surprised, and you keep most of your evenings.

choices.label: Turn it down
choices.result: You thank them and pass. Your evenings stay yours, and your bank account stays exactly where it was.

scenarios.title: The Loaner Car
scenarios.text: A car dealer who sits behind your bench every home game offers you a 'loaner' for the semester. No paperwork, he says, and nobody needs to know.

authoring.premise: A car dealer who sits behind the bench offers you a 'loaner' for the semester. No paperwork, he says.

choices.label: Turn him down flat
choices.result: You thank him and say you'll keep walking. He laughs it off, but he never brings it up again.

choices.label: Tell compliance about the offer
choices.result: You mention it to the compliance office so it's on record. They thank you, and the dealer's season tickets quietly move to the other side of the stadium.

choices.label: Take the keys
choices.result: You drive it for six weeks. Then a reporter photographs it in the athletes' lot, the plates trace back to the dealership, and you're walking again with a compliance meeting on your calendar.

scenarios.title: Conference Media Day
scenarios.text: The team picks you to speak at conference media day: live, a dozen microphones, and every question about whether a kicker can handle a big-time conference.

authoring.premise: The team picks you to speak at conference media day, live, with a dozen microphones in your face.

choices.label: Prepare three good answers
choices.result: You write out three answers and practice them in the mirror. On the day, you're calm, a little funny and nobody gets a headline out of you.

choices.label: Wing it with a smile
choices.result: You walk up without notes and say whatever comes to mind. One joke lands so well it ends up in every highlight package. One answer about a rival school gets passed around a lot too.

choices.label: Credit the whole unit
choices.result: You spend every answer talking about your snapper, your holder and the coverage team. The reporters get nothing spicy, and the specialists' group chat goes crazy.

scenarios.title: Rivalry Week
scenarios.text: Rivalry week: someone painted your team's statue in the other school's colors overnight. After curfew, a group of teammates plans a drive to their campus to hang your colors on the fence outside their stadium.

authoring.premise: Rivalry week: someone painted your statue overnight, and teammates plan a midnight trip to the other campus to return the favor.

choices.label: Stay in and keep it on the field
choices.result: You tell them the only answer that counts is Saturday's, then stay in and watch their special teams film. A few call you boring on Thursday. Nobody remembers that by Sunday.

choices.label: Make a better plan in daylight
choices.result: You talk the group into a legal version: a banner at your own student section and a video for the team's page. It's a hit, and nobody has to explain anything to anyone.

choices.label: Ride along after curfew
choices.result: You pile into the car at midnight and get back at three. By morning the other school has a photo of your crew on their fence, and so does your athletic director.

scenarios.title: The Alum in the League
scenarios.text: A kicker from your school who made it to the pros offers to train you for a week this summer, at his own cost. It's the same week as your family's reunion.

authoring.premise: A kicker from your school who made it to the pros offers to train you for a week this summer, at his own cost.

choices.label: Train with him
choices.result: You spend a week kicking with a pro: his warmup, his charting, his tricks for cold days. You come back with a notebook full of ideas and a phone number you'll use for years.

choices.label: Go to the reunion
choices.result: You choose the reunion and spend a week with cousins you haven't seen since high school. It's loud and warm, and you come back rested.

choices.label: Ask for film and notes instead
choices.result: You ask if he'd watch your film and send notes. He does, generously, and you split the week between the reunion and the backyard net.

scenarios.title: The Summer Plan
scenarios.text: Summer is three choices: summer classes to get ahead, a circuit of kicking camps, or a job back home that pays real money.

authoring.premise: Summer is three choices: summer classes to get ahead, a kicking camp circuit, or a job back home.

choices.label: Summer classes
choices.result: You stay on campus and take two classes. It's hot and quiet, and you start the fall a semester ahead.

choices.label: The kicking camp circuit
choices.result: You drive to four camps in six weeks and kick in front of coaches who've never heard of you. Your leg's never been more tired, or better.

choices.label: The job back home
choices.result: You work at the warehouse and kick in the park at night. You come back with money in the bank and calluses on the wrong body part.

choices.label: Job by day, your plan by night
choices.result: You take the job back home and run your own training plan every evening. It's exhausting, and it's the most complete summer you've had.
choices.lock_text: having built your own training plan before

scenarios.title: The Holder Who Wants Out
scenarios.text: {holder} wants to stop holding and focus on winning a starting job in the secondary. It means a new holder for you in the middle of the season.

authoring.premise: {holder} wants to stop holding to focus on winning a starting job elsewhere on the roster.

choices.label: Back {holder}'s decision
choices.result: You tell {holder} to go get the job and offer to help break in the replacement. It costs you two weeks of awkward holds.

choices.label: Ask {holder} to stay through the season
choices.result: You ask {holder} to hold until the season ends and chase the job in spring. {holder} agrees, a little reluctantly.

choices.label: Find a way to do both
choices.result: You go to {coach} with a plan: {holder} holds on game days and spends the rest of the week with the secondary. The coach is skeptical, then says yes.

scenarios.title: The Advisor's Warning
scenarios.text: {teacher} closes the office door and turns the screen around: one more bad grade this semester and you're academically ineligible. 'I can help,' your advisor says, 'but not if you keep hiding things from me.'

authoring.premise: {teacher} calls you in: one more bad grade and you're academically ineligible.

choices.label: Lay it all out
choices.result: You list every class, every missing assignment and every grade you were hoping nobody would see. {teacher} builds a plan with you on the spot, and you start it that night.

choices.label: Promise to handle it yourself
choices.result: You say you've got it under control and walk out with a list of tutoring hours you mean to use. Some weeks you do. The grade comes back just over the line.

choices.label: Drop the hardest class
choices.result: You drop the class that's sinking you and take the hit to your credit hours. You're safe this semester, though now you're behind for graduation.

scenarios.title: Hosting the Team Party
scenarios.text: Your apartment is the obvious place for the team party after the home opener, and everyone's already planning it in the group chat. Your lease has a noise clause, and your landlord lives downstairs.

authoring.premise: Your apartment is the obvious place for the team party, and everyone's already planning it.

choices.label: Host a team dinner instead
choices.result: You turn it into a dinner: pasta, music, cards, everyone out by eleven. It's smaller than the guys wanted, and half of them say it was the best night of the season.

choices.label: Say not at your place
choices.result: You tell the chat your place is off-limits this time. Someone else hosts, and you go for an hour.

choices.label: Throw the big one
choices.result: You host the biggest party of the fall. The noise complaint comes at one, campus security at two, and a letter from the athletic department by Wednesday.

scenarios.title: The Roommate Problem Grows
scenarios.text: Whatever you and your roommate had going, a deal or a cold war, is over: his late nights have turned into parties in your room three nights a week, and last night someone you've never met was asleep on your bed.

authoring.premise: Your roommate's late nights have turned into parties in your room three nights a week.

choices.label: Sit down and talk it out
choices.result: You catch him alone and tell him exactly how it's hitting your sleep and your season. He's embarrassed, and the parties move down the hall.

choices.label: Request a room change
choices.result: You fill out the housing form and move across campus a week later. New room, quiet nights, and a long walk to the dining hall.

choices.label: Join in if you can't sleep anyway
choices.result: You figure if you can't sleep, you might as well have fun. The nights are great; the mornings are brutal, the strength coach notices, and so do the teammates who keep covering your lifts.

scenarios.title: The Leadership Council
scenarios.text: {coach} invites you onto the team's leadership council, the players who set the team rules and deal with the problems before the coaches have to.

authoring.premise: {coach} invites you onto the team's leadership council, the players who set the rules and handle the problems.

choices.label: Join the council
choices.result: You say yes and spend Monday nights in a room with the captains, sorting out curfew fights and locker-room feuds. It's tedious, and it makes you see the whole team differently.

choices.label: Say you're not ready yet
choices.result: You tell {coach} you'd rather earn it with one more year. The coach respects the honesty and says the seat will be there.

choices.label: Bring what you learned as a captain
choices.result: You join and, at the first meeting, suggest the thing that worked for your high school unit: problems go to the players first. It sticks.
choices.lock_text: having led a team before

choices.label: Admit you got this wrong once
choices.result: You tell {coach} you once used a role like this to make your own life easier, and you want to do it differently this time. The coach puts you on the council anyway, because of that answer.
choices.lock_text: having misused a leadership role before

scenarios.title: The Head Coach Is Fired
scenarios.text: The head coach is fired the morning after the last game. Staff jobs are up in the air, {coach} may not be back, and half the roster is checking the transfer portal.

authoring.premise: The head coach is fired the morning after the last game. Staff jobs are up in the air, and half the roster is checking the portal.

choices.label: Stay and say so
choices.result: You tell {coach} and the athletic director you're staying, no matter who they hire. It's a bet on yourself and on this place.

choices.label: Look at your options
choices.result: You put your name in a few group chats and take a couple of calls, just to know what's out there. Nothing's decided, and the program notices.

choices.label: Wait and see who they hire
choices.result: You decide to wait for the new staff before deciding anything. It's sensible, and a lot of anxious weeks.

scenarios.title: The Fundraiser Nobody Wants to Run
scenarios.text: The children's hospital asks the team to run a kick-a-thon fundraiser: pledges per field goal in practice, kids on the sideline. Someone has to organize it, and nobody's volunteering.

authoring.premise: A children's hospital asks the team to run a kick-a-thon fundraiser. Someone has to organize it.

choices.label: Run it yourself
choices.result: You spend three weeks on sponsors, permits and pledge sheets. The kick-a-thon raises more than the hospital asked for, and two of the kids wear your number.

choices.label: Share it with the specialists
choices.result: You split the work with the punter and the snapper. It's smaller, and it gets done.

choices.label: Let someone else take it
choices.result: You say you're too busy this month, which is true. The event happens without you, and you watch it on someone else's phone.

choices.label: Bring in your old volunteer contacts
choices.result: You call the people you volunteered with back home, who know exactly how to run one of these. It's the best-run event the team's ever had.
choices.lock_text: having volunteered in your community before

scenarios.title: Spring Break
scenarios.text: Spring break, and teammates are going to the beach. Offseason lifts are optional that week, and so, it seems, are the team's rules.

authoring.premise: Teammates are going to the beach for spring break. Offseason lifts are optional that week, and so, it seems, are the rules.

choices.label: Go, and keep your rules
choices.result: You go, lift at the hotel gym every morning and are in bed before anything gets loud. You come back tan, rested and with nothing to explain.

choices.label: Stay on campus
choices.result: You stay and use the empty facility all week. It's quiet, a little lonely, and productive.

choices.label: Go all in
choices.result: You go to every party and stay out every night. On Thursday, the police break one up, and your name ends up on a list that gets back to {coach} before you do.

scenarios.title: The Kicking Camp Coach
scenarios.text: A private kicking coach who has sent players to the pros offers you a spot in his elite summer group, but only if you drop the school's summer program that {coach} runs.

authoring.premise: A private kicking coach who's sent players to the pros offers you a spot in his elite group, if you drop your school's summer program.

choices.label: Join the private group
choices.result: You join. The drills are brilliant, the price is high, and {coach} takes it personally.

choices.label: Stay with the school program
choices.result: You thank him and stay. The program is less flashy, and {coach} gives you more reps than ever.

choices.label: Ask {coach} to make it work
choices.result: You ask {coach} whether you could do the private group's first two weeks and then come back. It takes two meetings, and the coach agrees.

choices.label: Check his record first
choices.result: You call two of his former players before deciding. One loved him; one says he ruins hips. You stay with {coach} and borrow his best drill.
choices.lock_text: having checked out a trainer before trusting him

scenarios.title: The New Head Coach
scenarios.text: The new head coach starts with a team meeting and a new rulebook: phones in a basket, no hats indoors, every player at breakfast. He says he's already heard about every player on the roster.

authoring.premise: The new head coach, Marcus Reyes, starts with a team meeting and a new rulebook. He says he's heard about every player on the roster already.

choices.label: Buy in from day one
choices.result: You're at breakfast early every day for a month. The new staff notices, and so do the players who were waiting to see which way the room would go.

choices.label: Ask him what he heard about you
choices.result: You knock on his door and ask, straight out, what he's heard about you. He tells you, and it's fairer than you expected.

choices.label: Keep your head down
choices.result: You follow the new rules and say nothing. It's safe. It also means the new staff learns about you from other people.

scenarios.title: The Second Strike
scenarios.text: It happened again, and this time it isn't only the coaches who know. A local reporter has called the athletic department, {coach} says the team will put out a statement tonight, and teammates are already asking what you're going to say.

authoring.premise: It happens again. This time it isn't only the coaches who know: a reporter is asking questions, and the team has to respond.
authoring.note: Opens only on a strike AFTER the first warning: The Coach's Office clears every strike flag, so an old strike can't open it. Story event (x4 weight while open; forced in the last week of its window if the player qualifies): forced in year 4 week 6.

choices.label: Own it in your own words
choices.result: You sit down with {coach} and the media staff and write the statement yourself: what you did, that it was wrong, what you'll do now. It runs that night. It's humiliating, and people notice you didn't hide.

choices.label: Let the department answer
choices.result: You stay quiet and let a short, vague statement go out. The story fades in a few days, but inside the building people stop trusting what you say.

choices.label: Blame the people around you
choices.result: Off the record, you tell the reporter your teammates set you up. Your name is in the paper the next morning anyway, next to theirs. {coach} doesn't yell, and that's worse.

scenarios.title: The Runner
scenarios.text: A man in a nice jacket catches you in the parking lot after practice. He says he works 'with' an agent, hands you an envelope of cash and a new phone, and says there's more where that came from.

authoring.premise: A man who says he works 'with' an agent finds you after practice with cash, a new phone and a promise of more.

choices.label: Report him
choices.result: You hand the envelope back, take a photo of his license plate and walk straight to compliance. It's an awkward afternoon of forms, and your name never comes up in the story that follows.

choices.label: Hand it back and walk away
choices.result: You give it all back and say no thanks. He smiles like he'll try again, and you don't tell anyone.

choices.label: Keep the envelope
choices.result: You keep the cash and the phone. Three weeks later compliance calls you in: the runner's other players talked, and your name is on a list you can't explain.

scenarios.title: The Captain's Vote
scenarios.text: Captain voting is next week, and someone has written your name on the ballot. Kickers almost never get the votes, but a few teammates say this year could be different.
