authoring.premise: The team votes for captains, and your name is on the ballot.

choices.label: Run for it
choices.result: You say yes and spend the week talking to every position group, not about you but about what the team needs. The vote is close, and when it's counted, you've got the patch.

choices.label: Back someone else
choices.result: You take your name off the ballot and tell the room to vote for the senior linebacker who has earned it. He wins, and he remembers who stood up for him.

choices.label: Stay out of it
choices.result: You leave your name off and skip the speeches. You spend the extra hour in the film room every night that week instead.

choices.label: Ask {coach} first
choices.result: You've had a coach who trusted you completely, and you want that again. You ask {coach} what a captain from the specialists would need to do, then run on that answer and win.
choices.lock_text: having earned a coach's full confidence before

scenarios.title: The Captain's Burden
scenarios.text: A starting linebacker missed curfew on a road trip, and the coaches don't know yet. He finds you in the hotel hallway and asks you, as one of the team's leaders, to keep it in the locker room.

authoring.premise: A teammate breaks team rules and asks you, as captain, to keep it in the locker room.

choices.label: Give him until breakfast
choices.result: You tell him he has until breakfast to tell {coach} himself, or you will. He tells. He's furious for a week, and then he starts showing up early.

choices.label: Handle it player to player
choices.result: You make him run the stadium stairs with you at six the next morning and leave the coaches out of it. The room respects it, and the coaches never hear a thing.

choices.label: Let it go
choices.result: You tell him not to let it happen again and leave it there. It doesn't come up again, but two younger players saw the whole thing.

scenarios.title: The Scouting Questionnaire
scenarios.text: A pro team sends you its first questionnaire: forty questions about your family, your habits and your goals. Question 14 asks you to describe any off-field incidents in your college career.

authoring.premise: A pro team sends a questionnaire. Question 14: 'Describe any off-field incidents in your college career.'

choices.label: Answer every question straight
choices.result: Whatever belongs on the page, you write it plainly, including the parts you'd rather forget, and ask {coach} to read it before you send it. It isn't all flattering, and it's all true.

choices.label: Shade a few answers
choices.result: You leave a couple of things out and soften the rest. It reads well. Whether it matches what the scouts already know is another question.

choices.label: Leave it for next year
choices.result: You put it in a drawer: it's a junior-year questionnaire, and you have midterms. The team's scout notes that you never sent it back.

choices.label: Add a page about what you stand for
choices.result: You answer the hard questions, then add a page about what you want from a pro career and what you won't do for one. A scout calls just to say nobody has ever sent that page before.
choices.lock_text: having been clear about what you wanted in recruiting

scenarios.title: The Agent's Dinner
scenarios.text: An agent you've never met invites you to the best steakhouse in town to 'talk about your future,' and he's picking up the check. It's a year before you're allowed to sign with anyone, and you both know the rules.

authoring.premise: An agent invites you to a steakhouse to 'talk about your future.' It's a year too early, and you both know the rules.

choices.label: Decline and wait
choices.result: You thank him, say you'll talk after your last game like the rules say, and mention the invitation to {coach}. He says he respects that. He also says the offer won't be this good next year.

choices.label: Go to dinner, sign nothing
choices.result: You eat the steak, listen to the pitch and leave without signing anything. It's within the rules, barely, and his texts start arriving every week after.

choices.label: Shake on a secret deal
choices.result: He slides an envelope across the table, a 'loan' against your future, and you shake on a deal nobody can know about. You spend the summer checking your phone for a compliance email.

scenarios.title: The Transfer Kicker
scenarios.text: A kicker with a big resume transfers in from another school, and the coaches love his leg. {coach} says the job is open again.

authoring.premise: A kicker with a big resume transfers in from another school, and the coaches love his leg.

choices.label: Compete for it
choices.result: You out-prepare everyone: film, sleep, charts. You don't say a word about the transfer, good or bad, and {coach} notices that too.

choices.label: Welcome him in
choices.result: You show the transfer around and invite him to the specialists' dinner. It's strange to help the person chasing your job, and the room respects it.

choices.label: Make his life harder
choices.result: You 'forget' to tell him about schedule changes and move his ball bag twice. He figures it out in a week, and so does {coach}.

choices.label: Do what you did in high school
choices.result: You helped a rival for your job once and it made you both better. You split warmups with the transfer and push each other every day.
choices.lock_text: having helped a teammate who was competing with you

scenarios.title: The Long Way Back
scenarios.text: You've got a reputation now, and the staff is watching. {coach} offers one way back: 6 a.m. workouts with the strength staff, twenty community hours, and no more excuses for the rest of the year.

authoring.premise: You've got a reputation now, and the staff is watching. {coach} offers one path back: early workouts, community hours, and no more excuses.
authoring.note: Story event (x4 weight while open; forced in the last week of its window if the player qualifies): forced in year 4 week 8.

choices.label: Take every hour of it
choices.result: You show up at six every day for a semester, finish the community hours early and keep your name out of every story. In the spring, {coach} tells a visiting scout you're not the same player, and means it.

choices.label: Do the minimum
choices.result: You do the workouts you can't skip and the hours you can't avoid. Nothing new goes wrong, but nothing changes either, and the label stays.

choices.label: Tell {coach} you've already paid for it
choices.result: You say you've served your time and don't need a program. {coach} closes the folder and says that's your choice. It's the last offer you get.

scenarios.title: The Mental Health Day
scenarios.text: You're tired in a way sleep doesn't fix. This morning you sat in the car outside the facility for twenty minutes before you could make yourself go in. The team counselor stops you in the hallway and says taking a day isn't weakness.

authoring.premise: You're exhausted in a way sleep doesn't fix. The team counselor says taking a day isn't weakness.

choices.label: Take the day
choices.result: You tell {coach} you need a day, and the coach just says okay. You sleep, call home and walk for an hour without your phone. The next morning, the drive in is just a drive.

choices.label: Push through it
choices.result: You go in anyway and get every rep. Nobody notices anything is wrong, which is the problem.

choices.label: Book a session with the counselor
choices.result: You don't take the day, but you take the counselor's Thursday slot. Talking it through doesn't fix the week. It does make it feel smaller.

scenarios.title: The Old Injury Returns
scenarios.text: The groin strain is back, worse this time, right before the conference schedule. The trainer wants two weeks of rehab, and you can feel it on every kickoff.

authoring.premise: The groin strain is back, worse this time, right before the conference schedule.

choices.label: Do the full two weeks
choices.result: You do every band, every ice bath and every boring stretch for two weeks. It's slow and maddening, and the strain is gone when it's over.

choices.label: Rehab and kick short
choices.result: You rehab in the mornings and kick only short field goals in practice. You keep your timing, and the strain stays exactly where it was.

choices.label: Tape it and keep going
choices.result: You tape it, take the full load and say nothing. The leg holds for now, and it hurts more every week.

choices.label: Tell them everything this time
choices.result: You hid an injury once and paid for it. This time you tell the trainer everything, including the parts you'd usually leave out, and the plan fits exactly what's wrong.
choices.lock_text: having hidden an injury before

scenarios.title: A High School Teammate Calls
scenarios.text: Someone from your old high school team calls: they're visiting campus next weekend for a college visit and need a place to stay and a tour.

authoring.premise: Someone from your old high school team calls: they're visiting campus next weekend and need a place to stay and a tour.

choices.label: Host them all weekend
choices.result: You give up your bed, show them every corner of campus and introduce them to half the team. They leave saying they want to come here.

choices.label: Give them one good afternoon
choices.result: You give the tour on Saturday, buy lunch and point them to a hotel. It's friendly, and you keep your weekend.

choices.label: Say it's a bad weekend
choices.result: You say it's a bad weekend, which is true. They understand, and you feel a little bad about it.

choices.label: Give them the visit you wish you'd had
choices.result: You helped a freshman find their way in high school, so you plan the visit you wish you'd had: real questions, honest answers, no sales pitch.
choices.lock_text: having helped a younger player find their way before

scenarios.title: Trouble at Home
scenarios.text: {sibling} got suspended from school for a fight. {parent} calls, overwhelmed, and asks you to talk to him.

authoring.premise: {sibling} got suspended from school for a fight. {parent} is overwhelmed and asks you to talk to him.

choices.label: Call {sibling} that night
choices.result: You call and mostly listen. It turns out the fight was about someone saying something about {parent}. You don't excuse it, and you don't lecture.

choices.label: Give him a hard talk
choices.result: You tell {sibling} he's better than this and there's no excuse. He goes quiet and says 'okay' too fast.

choices.label: Invite him up for a weekend
choices.result: You ask {parent} to send {sibling} to campus for the weekend. You take him to practice and let the linemen talk to him, which works better than anything you could say.

scenarios.title: {parent}'s Health Scare
scenarios.text: A late-night call: {parent} is in the hospital. They think it's his heart. You're four hundred miles away, and there's a game on Saturday.

authoring.premise: A late-night call: {parent} is in the hospital. They think it's his heart, and you're four hundred miles away with a game Saturday.

choices.label: Go home now
choices.result: You tell {coach} and take the first flight out. You sit with {parent} for two days, fly back Friday night and barely sleep before the game.

choices.label: Stay and call every hour
choices.result: {sibling} is there, and {parent} insists you stay. You call every few hours and stare at your phone through every meeting.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what to do
choices.result: You go to {coach}'s office at midnight. The coach says family first and books the flight before you can argue.

choices.label: Ask {parent} what he needs
choices.result: You ask {parent}, plainly, whether he wants you there. He says yes, which he's never said before. You're on the plane by morning.
choices.lock_text: having learned to talk openly with your family

scenarios.title: The Integrity Hearing
scenarios.text: Your professor has reported the paper. The hearing is next Tuesday: three faculty members, the paper on the table, and {teacher} in the chair beside you as your advisor.

authoring.premise: Your professor reports a possible academic integrity violation. The hearing is next week.

choices.label: Admit it and accept the sanction
choices.result: You tell the panel exactly what happened before they ask. You get a zero on the paper and a semester of integrity workshops, and {teacher} says it's the first hearing in years where nobody had to drag the truth out.

choices.label: Ask {teacher} to speak for you

scenarios.title: The Holder's Future

scenarios.title: What Comes After

authoring.premise: {love_interest} asks the question you've both avoided: what happens to us after college?

scenarios.title: {parent} at Every Game

scenarios.title: The Little Brother's Recruiting

authoring.premise: {sibling} is a high school senior now, and college coaches are calling. He asks you how to handle them.

scenarios.title: The Mental Toll
scenarios.text: Draft calls, final exams and your last season are all happening at once. You've snapped at {holder} twice this week, you haven't slept a full night in a month, and you don't feel like yourself.

scenarios.title: The Last Injury Scare
scenarios.text: Your knee buckles on a routine practice kick three weeks before the scouts' workout. It holds, mostly. The trainer wants an MRI.

authoring.premise: Your knee buckles on a routine practice kick three weeks before scouts arrive.

choices.label: Say nothing and keep kicking

scenarios.title: Final Exams, Final Season

authoring.premise: Your last finals land in the same week as your last regular-season game.

choices.label: Study on the bus and the plane
choices.result: You turn every trip into a study session and get four hours of sleep a night. You pass everything, and you're exhausted on Saturday.

choices.result: You ask {teacher} to arrange makeup times with your professors. It takes three emails each, and you get a normal week.

choices.label: Take every exam by the book

choices.lock_text: having sat through an integrity hearing

scenarios.title: The Senior Trip

choices.label: Stay the whole weekend

authoring.premise: A national brand wants an exclusive NIL deal for your senior year. It pays more than everything else combined, and it ends all your local deals.

scenarios.title: Giving Back

scenarios.title: The Scout's Dinner

choices.label: Play, carefully
choices.result: You play half-speed, take the open jumpers and stay out of the paint. Nobody gets hurt, and you're on the group chat's highlight reel.

choices.label: Keep score instead
choices.result: You run the scoreboard and the trash talk. It's almost as fun, and your ankles thank you.

choices.label: Pass and stretch instead
choices.result: You say no and spend the afternoon on mobility work. Your hips feel great, and the stories from the game are very loud at dinner.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Crowd
scenarios.text: A group of friends from outside the team goes out every night, and they've started inviting you along: never pushy, always fun, every single night.

authoring.premise: A group of non-team friends parties every night, and they've started inviting you along.

choices.label: Go out with them every time
choices.result: You become a regular. Your grades slide, you're late twice, and {coach} starts hearing your name from people who aren't on the team.

choices.label: See them on weekends only
choices.result: You tell them weekdays are off-limits and stick to it. They tease you about it, and they still invite you on Saturdays.

choices.label: Say no and mean it
choices.result: You say thanks, but it's not your life right now. They stop asking after a week, and your evenings get quiet again.

scenarios.title: The Borrowed Car
scenarios.text: A teammate wants to borrow your car for the night. He won't say where he's going, and he's already holding out his hand for the keys.

authoring.premise: A teammate wants to borrow your car for the night and won't say where he's going.

choices.label: Say no
choices.result: You say no, nicely, and offer to drive him wherever it is tomorrow. He's annoyed and finds another ride.

choices.label: Drive him yourself
choices.result: You say you'll drive. It's a ride to his girlfriend's place across town, and you're back in an hour.

choices.label: Hand him the keys
choices.result: You toss him the keys. The car comes back at 4 a.m. with a parking ticket and a dent, and you never find out where it was.

scenarios.title: The Camp You Run
scenarios.text: Parents back home offer you cash to run private kicking lessons for their kids this summer. Compliance has rules about that, and the money is good.

authoring.premise: Parents offer you cash to run private kicking lessons for their kids this summer. Compliance has rules about that.

choices.label: Take the cash and skip the paperwork
choices.result: You run the lessons and take cash. In the fall, one parent posts a thank-you online, and compliance asks to see your paperwork.

choices.label: Run it through compliance
choices.result: You fill out the forms and run the lessons the legal way. It takes a week to get approved and pays a little less.

choices.label: Teach for free
choices.result: You run a few free lessons at the local field instead. No forms, no money, a lot of happy kids.

scenarios.title: The Aid Office Error
scenarios.text: The financial aid office deposits twice what you're owed this semester. Nobody has noticed yet.

authoring.premise: The financial aid office deposits twice what you're owed.

choices.label: Report it right away
choices.result: You call the aid office the same day. They thank you, fix it, and you go back to being exactly as broke as before.

choices.label: Leave it until they notice
choices.result: You don't touch it and don't report it. Two months later they notice, take it back, and charge a late fee for your trouble.

choices.label: Spend some of it
choices.result: You spend part of it on new cleats and a nice dinner. When the aid office asks for it back, you don't have it, and the repayment plan runs all semester.

scenarios.title: The Extension
scenarios.text: Team travel lands right on a paper deadline. A teammate says the trick is to email the professor about a family emergency; nobody ever checks.

authoring.premise: Team travel lands on a paper deadline. A teammate says the trick is to claim a family emergency.

choices.label: Claim the family emergency
choices.result: You send the email. The professor gives you a week and sends a kind note about your family. Then {teacher} gets a call about it, and the story doesn't hold.

choices.label: Ask for an extension honestly
choices.result: You email the professor about the travel and ask for two days. You get them, and the paper is better for it.

choices.label: Finish it early
choices.result: You write it in three late nights before the trip. It's not your best work, and it's on time, with the whole trip free for film.

scenarios.title: The Coach From Home
scenarios.text: Your old high school coach is in town and stops by to watch you practice. It's the first time in years you've kicked in front of the person who taught you most of it.

authoring.premise: Your high school coach visits campus and wants to watch you practice.

choices.label: Ask for notes
choices.result: After practice you ask your old coach to be honest about your form. The notes are short and sharp, and two of them stick.

choices.label: Introduce them to {coach}
choices.result: You introduce your old coach to {coach}, and the two of them talk kicking for an hour while you stand there grinning.

choices.label: Take them to dinner
choices.result: You skip the film session to take your old coach to dinner. You talk about everything except kicking, and it's the best night of your month.

choices.label: Say thank you properly
choices.result: You tell your old coach, out loud, what that trust meant to you. They don't say much back. They don't have to.
choices.lock_text: having earned your high school coach's confidence

scenarios.title: The Hospital Visit
scenarios.text: The team visits a children's hospital. Some players are there for the cameras, and when the cameras leave, a kid in a wheelchair asks you to stay and play a video game.

authoring.premise: The team visits a children's hospital. Some players are there for the cameras; one kid asks you to stay longer.

choices.label: Stay and play
choices.result: You stay two extra hours and lose every game. The kid's mother writes the team a letter, and you keep a copy.

choices.label: Promise to come back
choices.result: You have to leave with the team, so you promise to come back next week, and you do. Then the week after that, and two teammates start coming with you.

choices.label: Leave with the bus
choices.result: You say a warm goodbye and get on the bus with everyone else. You think about that kid for the whole ride home.

scenarios.title: The Weekend Off
scenarios.text: Friends from home invite you to a lake cabin for a weekend off, the first one you've had in months. It's quiet, with no plan except fishing and sleep.

authoring.premise: Friends invite you away for a weekend off, your first in months.

choices.label: Go and actually rest
choices.result: You go, sleep ten hours a night and leave your phone in the car. You come back feeling like a person again.

choices.label: Go, and bring the kicking net
choices.result: You go and set up a net behind the cabin. It's half a vacation, and your friends think it's hilarious.

choices.label: Stay and train
choices.result: You skip it and spend the weekend at the facility. It's productive, and the photos from the lake look perfect.

scenarios.title: The Next Level
scenarios.text: The last week of your college career. Whatever happens on draft day, this is where the kicker you became walks off the field. {parent} is waiting by the tunnel, and {coach} has one question for you: 'What's next?'

authoring.premise: The last week of your college career. Whatever happens on draft day, this is where the kicker you became walks off the field.
authoring.note: Locked choices: ready_for_pros needs combine_ready or pro_day_ready; life_after_football needs finished_degree_track; a rebuilt_reputation lock adds 'the long way back'; still_proving_it is open.

choices.label: Say you're ready for the pros
choices.result: You tell {coach} you've done everything you can and you're ready for whoever calls. {parent} hears it and nods like he's known for years.
choices.lock_text: having prepared for the scouts

choices.label: Say you'll be okay either way
choices.result: You tell them football is the plan and the degree is the backup, and you mean both. Whatever the phone does on draft day, you'll be okay.
choices.lock_text: having stayed on track for your degree

choices.label: Say you're still proving it
choices.result: You tell {coach} you're not done proving anything, to the scouts or to yourself. The coach smiles: 'Good. Keep that.'

choices.label: Say thank you first
choices.result: You don't answer the question yet. You thank {coach}, then walk over and hug {parent} for a long time. 'What's next' can wait a week.

scenarios.title: Who's Driving?
scenarios.text: The party is breaking up, and the teammate who drove you here has had too much. He's jingling his keys at the door and telling everyone to pile in.

authoring.premise: A teammate who has had too much insists on driving everyone home from a party. You're one of his passengers.

choices.label: Find another way home
choices.result: You say you'll find your own ride, then call a car for yourself and two freshmen who were about to get in. It costs you twenty dollars and some teasing. On Monday, one freshman's mother emails {coach} to say thank you.

choices.label: Ride along
choices.result: You get in the back seat because everyone else does. Four blocks later, police lights fill the car. Nobody's hurt, and every name in that car is in the paper by Tuesday, yours included.

choices.label: Take the keys and drive
choices.result: You haven't had anything all night, so you take his keys and drive everyone home yourself. He calls you a narc in front of the whole party and doesn't speak to you for a week.

scenarios.title: The Balcony Dare
scenarios.text: Spring trip, a hotel by the beach. A friend leans over the third-floor balcony rail, points at the pool below and offers you a hundred dollars to jump. Somebody already has a phone out.

authoring.premise: On a spring trip, a friend dares you to jump from the hotel balcony into the pool three floors down.
authoring.note: Offseason after years 1-3 (spring break and summer trips). The jump is a strike with a real injury.

choices.label: Say no and take the stairs
choices.result: You laugh, say you like your legs where they are and take the stairs down to the pool. You swim, you sleep, and you fly home with nothing to explain.

choices.label: Stop him from trying it
choices.result: When you say no, he starts climbing the rail himself. You pull him back by the shirt and walk him inside. He's angry for ten minutes and grateful for the rest of the trip.

choices.label: Jump
choices.result: You climb the rail and jump. You're a foot short of where you thought you'd land, clip the pool's edge and spend the night in an emergency room. The video is online before your X-ray comes back, and {coach} sees both.

scenarios.title: The Keys
scenarios.text: You're the one who stayed sober tonight, so the host gave you a teammate's car keys at midnight for safekeeping. Now he's in no shape to drive, he's standing in front of you, and he wants them back.

authoring.premise: After a party, a teammate who is in no shape to drive demands his keys back. You're sober, and you're holding them.

choices.label: Keep the keys and call a ride
choices.result: You put the keys in your pocket and call him a car. He argues in the driveway for ten minutes, then falls asleep in the back seat. You hand the keys back at breakfast.

choices.label: Hand them back and let him go
choices.result: You give him the keys because it's easier than the fight, and he drives off alone. He wrecks the car against a light pole a mile away with nobody else in it and walks away bruised. By morning, everyone knows who gave him the keys back, and so does {coach}.

choices.label: Drive him home yourself
choices.result: You drive him home in his own car, walk him to his door and walk two miles back at 2 a.m. You get four hours of sleep, and some teammates think you overstepped. He gets home safe.

scenarios.title: The Fast Lane
scenarios.text: Driving back to campus late on a Sunday, a teammate pulls up next to you on the empty highway, revs his engine and points at the next exit sign. He wants a race.

authoring.premise: A teammate pulls up next to you on the highway at night and dares you to race him to the next exit.

choices.label: Let him go
choices.result: You ease off the gas and watch his taillights disappear. He texts you a chicken emoji. You get home in one piece, with a clean record.

choices.label: Call him when you're both home
choices.result: You let him go, then call him once you're both home and tell him he scared you. He laughs it off, but he drives the speed limit to practice all week.

choices.label: Race him
choices.result: You floor it. A state trooper clocks you both at 102, the tickets come with a court date, and the local news runs the story with your team photo. {coach} reads it before you're out of bed.
